Incident log evidence files and server/container console exports
Original log event with source line/range and recorded timestamp
Human-readable configurable detection rules with version
Failed SSH or organizer-admin authentication events
Suspected shell-command injection indicators in logged input
Per-run audit findings, analyst reports and manifest
Future supplied sanitized logs and labeled acceptance data plus synthetic samples
Linux investigation hosts and offline/local evidence boundary

Outputs.label: Runnable Python 3.12+ Linux CLI with source code
requirements: Offline/local auditing, supported SSH/syslog, Nginx, Apache, application/container console, plain and gzip logs
Large-volume memory-bounded ingestion; document supported variants; safe regex configuration and CLI/run statuses

Outputs.label: Default editable human-readable detection rules
requirements: Safe validation and regression-test fixtures; explicit limits and exclusions

Outputs.label: Per-run classified findings JSON Lines
requirements: One record per classified failed login or suspected injection finding with rule attribution, source provenance, timestamps and redacted excerpts
Preserve distinction between unique events and per-rule matches

Outputs.label: Per-run readable analyst report
requirements: Report counts, origin IPs, targeted accounts/endpoints, temporal distribution, clusters and manual-review records
Prefer CSV plus concise Markdown or HTML; defensible timeline and grouping explanations; redaction

Outputs.label: Per-run machine-readable run manifest
requirements: Input inventory, file SHA-256s, rule/config version, run times, tool version, examined records, parse failures, detections, final status
Clearly flag incomplete/warning/failed runs; separate partial from finalized outputs

Outputs.label: Test and benchmark evidence
requirements: Synthetic benign/malicious logs and automated tests; client-labeled acceptance data when later provided
False positives and misses, known detection limitations, busy-event comparable processing time and peak memory

Outputs.label: Operator and technical documentation
requirements: Install, command-line operation, configuration, troubleshooting, supported log formats and patterns
Security normalization limits, regex safeguards, privacy/redaction, incomplete-result handling, manual-investigation cases

object.value: For an online ticketing/event-management platform with Linux servers and containers, build a forensic triage tool to turn diverse logs into reliable, reviewable leads about failed logins and suspected shell injection.
Support reconstruction of what happened, when, targeted systems, and which actual log records warrant human investigation; do not assume two suspicious activities are related or an attack succeeded.
Investigate SSH authentication, reverse-proxy HTTP access and application/container console log evidence with varying formats, timestamps, duplicate lines, truncated/malformed lines.
Do not declare a breach, successful exploitation or compromised system merely from suspicious strings.
Accept one input export, multiple individually selected files, or a directory of incident evidence.
Support common syslog-style Linux SSH/authentication records.
Support Nginx and Apache HTTP access logs in documented supported layouts.
Support application or container console exports, with configurable patterns for timestamps and event boundaries.
Support plain-text logs and gzip-compressed exports where applicable.
Process large collections from several dozen systems without loading all evidence into RAM at once.
Explain read/unreadable files, recognized formats, and uninterpretable records.
Support documented multiline messages and extra terminal prefixes without inventing missing data.
Flag any unreliably parsed record as unclassified and account for it; never silently discard.
Identify actual failed SSH logins and actual failed organizer-admin application sign-ins.
Distinguish SSH Failed password, explicit application authentication failures and ordinary HTTP 401 responses; a 401 does not automatically establish failed authentication.
Base failed-login classification on source format and surrounding fields.
Extract source address, account identifier, target service, server and timestamp when present.
Mark absent authentication field values as unavailable; never fabricate them.
Highlight repeated authentication failures against the same account.
Highlight many distinct targeted accounts from one origin (password spraying pattern).
Highlight short-window failed-authentication bursts across servers.
Make event-count and time-window thresholds configurable without source edits.
Keep each individual event available as evidence alongside aggregated pattern summaries.
Evaluate HTTP request parameters, headers and application-log fields for suspected hostile input.
Use documented configurable regular expressions for suspicious shell command-execution syntax, metacharacter combinations, command substitution and relevant encoded forms.
Require field context and the complete rule condition; a lone semicolon, dollar sign or other punctuation must not automatically become a security incident.
Attach individually identifiable matching rules and explanations.
For supported URL-encoded fields, analyze a carefully normalized copy along with the recorded original.
Document bounded normalization; reject/handle ambiguous or excessively nested encoding safely and never overwrite original data.
Unless independent execution evidence exists, label matches suspected injection attempts or indicators for review, not proof of execution.
Do not perform exploit testing or vulnerability scanning.
For a selected incident window, show relevant events in chronological order and indicate each source.
Handle UTC, local and missing-offset timestamps; document assumptions.
Do not manufacture precise times when offsets or usable timestamps are unavailable.
Report source IPs with the most failed-login events.
Report whether multiple organizer accounts were targeted from a single origin.
Show endpoints receiving suspected shell-injection requests.
Examine proximity of suspicious HTTP requests to repeated auth failures without claiming causality.
Show systems and original source files behind relevant findings.
Never equate IP overlap/time proximity with common attacker identity; explain grouping rule and evidence.
Human-readable configuration for rule ID, description, applicable source types/fields, regex pattern, enabled status, and severity or review priority.
Support tuning, enabling and disabling rules without editing core parsing code.
Reject invalid rule configs with actionable explanations before auditing begins.
Attribute each match to the exact rule version/configuration used in that run.
Treat log text as hostile; use documented validation, input limits, timeouts or equivalent controls against catastrophic regex processing and resource exhaustion.
Never execute commands or other instructions present in input log content.
Each finding refers to original source file, determinable line or bounded range, recorded timestamp, extracted fields, matching rule, rationale, and short excerpt.
Include SHA-256 checksum for each audited evidence file.
Output JSON Lines with every classified failed-login or suspected-injection finding, including provenance and rule information.
Produce readable counts, leading sources, targeted accounts/endpoints, time distribution, notable clusters and records needing manual review.
Prefer CSV plus concise Markdown or HTML report; report must be readable.
Machine-readable manifest records inputs, file hashes, rules configuration version, run start/end, records examined, parse failures, detection counts, tool version and final status.
Clearly distinguish unique matched events from total individual rule matches where one event matches several rules.
Include source lines/records that could not be classified in run statistics.
Do not silently append earlier incident findings into a new investigation.
With same inputs and rule configuration, reproduce substantive findings apart from run-specific metadata.
Do not expose raw credentials, session tokens or other secrets in ordinary report files and console progress.
Mask sensitive portions of excerpts while retaining enough detection context for an analyst.
Do not alter or rewrite original input evidence files.
Never upload logs or other incident evidence to external services during auditing.
Do not download new detection rules during an audit.
Safely handle untrusted filenames, terminal escape sequences and recorded text in displays/exports.
Unreadable files and lost or interrupted processing prevent an audit being reported as fully complete; flag incomplete audit conspicuously.
Distinguish partial/interrupted output files from finalized results.
Use Python 3.12 or later with a Linux-compatible CLI.
Allow operators to choose input, output, rule configuration and optional time window.

Illustrative invocation: python auditor.py --input ./incident-evidence --rules ./rules.yaml --from 2026-10-17T00:00:00Z --to 2026-10-19T23:59:59Z --output ./audit-results; this is an example, not a prescribed incident window.
Provide periodic high-level progress, not an output of every analyzed event.
Meaningfully distinguish completed, completed-with-warnings, failed CLI exit codes.
Provide clear handling instructions/diagnostics for missing files, permissions, bad rules, corrupt archives and interruptions.
Dashboard, database server, alerting service and automatic IP blocking are NOT required in first release; prioritize repeatable offline analysis.
Before acceptance, incorporate client-provided sanitized real-format samples and an analyst-annotated investigation set; future evidence is not a precompile blocker.
Provide benign and malicious synthetic log examples for tests without requiring customer data.
Automated acceptance coverage: Positive failed logons, successful logins and unrelated auth errors.
Automated acceptance coverage: Repeated-account attacks and multi-account password spray.
Automated acceptance coverage: Suspicious shell strings and harmless punctuation.
Automated acceptance coverage: URL encoding, malformed escape sequences and evasion variants.
Automated acceptance coverage: Broken/missing timestamps, encodings, multiline console lines, truncated and corrupt gzip logs.
Automated acceptance coverage: Invalid/costly regex rules and long attacker-controlled fields.
Automated acceptance coverage: Overlapping duplicate exports, ordering across files and unmatched events.
Automated acceptance coverage: Permission failures, interruptions, deterministic reruns and preserved source hashes.
Automated acceptance coverage: Report redaction, line/range traceability and reproducible rule explanations.
Measure false positives and missed cases against labeled test data; report detection performance.
Disclose what rules cannot detect; never claim comprehensive detection of every injection attempt.
Benchmark bundle comparable to a busy event weekend on standard investigation host, capturing elapsed processing time and peak resident memory.
Demonstrate continued operation as log volume grows without merely running out of memory on oversized files.
Provide functioning application, source, CLI entry, default/editable regex rules, synthetic logs, automated tests, sample reports, benchmark results, install/operation/troubleshooting docs.
Document supported formats, patterns, known limitations, incomplete-result behavior and occasions requiring manual investigation.
Acceptance workflow: analyst processes an unfamiliar supported incident bundle via one documented command to obtain reproducible investigation package.
Detect labeled failed logins and suspicious injection indicators with disclosed limitations and false positives available for review.
Minimize irrelevant alerts with source-aware detection, expose remaining false positives.
Finding references/checksums verify every source finding.
Patterns and chronological evidence must be defensible.
Large audits stay bounded-memory, disclose unreadable material rather than omitting.
Do not characterize unverified indicators as proved compromise.
The application does not block attacks, decide that an incident is closed or replace the human analyst.
High-priority incident context: unexplained organizer-account lockouts and suspicious HTTP web requests.

During a recent high-traffic event weekend, organizers saw lockouts after failed sign-ins and unusual request parameters were observed at a public troubleshooting endpoint; relationship/success unknown.

Implement memory-bounded ingestion of selected files, folders and compressed evidence
Parse supported log formats, event boundaries, timestamps and source provenance without guessing
Implement configurable, validated, safe, traceable detection rules and thresholds
Classify genuine failed SSH and organizer-admin sign-in events, distinguish other responses/errors
Identify context-aware suspected shell injection indicators while retaining unmodified source
Summarize failure patterns, related-event evidence and a defensible incident timeline
Record original evidence traceability, file hashes and explainable unique-event versus match counts
Protect secrets, evidence, untrusted display text and local-only processing
Produce machine-readable JSON Lines classified findings with provenance and rules
Produce readable analyst summary including manual-review and cluster details
Produce machine-readable run manifest with source hashes, counts, version and status
Implement CLI run controls, safe finalization, diagnostics, progress and exit codes
Validate parsing, detection, privacy, edge cases, reporting and source-preservation with test sets
Measure detection metrics and benchmark throughput and peak memory on representative evidence
Package source, runnable CLI, rule definitions, synthetic tests, examples and documentation

objective: Compile the attached client requirements into a future execution contract for a repeatable, offline, evidence-preserving Python 3.12+ Security Log Regex Auditor for Linux investigators: identify genuine failed authentication and suspected shell injection, enable defensible triage and validation without asserting compromise or executing attacks.
